title: Answering OQ-03: Elementary ≡ 1 (mod 4) Proof
body:
**Open question from infinitude-primes-4k3**: Can the Euclid-style argument for primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) be adapted to prove infinitely many primes ≡ 1 (mod 4)?

**Answer: Yes**, but with a different construction. The ≡ 3 proof uses N = 4(n+1)! − 1 (which is ≡ 3 mod 4 and forces a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 by a product argument). For ≡ 1, we use N = (2(n+1)!)² + 1 — any odd prime p dividing this satisfies p² ≡ −1 (mod p), so −1 is a quadratic residue mod p, which by Euler's criterion forces p ≡ 1 (mod 4).

The ≡ 1 case requires deeper arithmetic: Euler's criterion, not just closure under multiplication.

title: The Two Constructions Compared
body:
The module comment shows both proofs side-by-side:

| | Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) | Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) |
|-|---------------------|---------------------|
| Construction | 4(n+1)! − 1 | (2(n+1)!)² + 1 |
| Key insight | Product of 1 mod 4 stays 1 mod 4 | Primes dividing k²+1 are ≡ 1 mod 4 |
| Difficulty | Elementary multiplication | Euler's criterion |

Both constructions ensure the candidate N has a prime factor with the target residue AND is larger than n (because any factor ≤ n would divide (n+1)! and hence divide N ∓ 1 = ±1, contradiction).

title: infinitely_many_primes_1_mod_4 — The OQ Answer
body:
```lean
theorem infinitely_many_primes_1_mod_4 :
    ∀ n : ℕ, ∃ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p ∧ p > n ∧ p % 4 = 1 :=
  InfinitudePrimes4k1.infinitely_many_primes_1_mod_4
```

This delegates directly to the proof in `InfinitudePrimes4k1.lean`. The proof is fully verified: 0 sorries, 0 axioms. The key steps are:
1. Take N = (2·(n+1)!)² + 1
2. N is odd and > 1, so has an odd prime factor p
3. By `prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four`: p ≡ 1 (mod 4)
4. If p ≤ n then p | (n+1)!, so p | N − 1 = (2(n+1)!)², forcing p | 1 — contradiction

The `prime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four` lemma uses `Nat.Prime.mod_four_ne_three_of_dvd_isSquare_neg_one` from Mathlib's SumTwoSquares module, which encodes Euler's criterion.

title: Complete mod-4 Classification of Primes
body:
```lean
theorem both_classes_infinite :
    Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | Nat.Prime p ∧ p % 4 = 1} ∧
    Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | Nat.Prime p ∧ p % 4 = 3}

theorem odd_prime_mod_four_classification :
    p % 4 = 1 ∨ p % 4 = 3  -- for any odd prime p
```

**The complete picture**: Every prime is either 2 (even) or odd. Every odd prime $p$ has $p \bmod 4 \in \{0,1,2,3\}$; since $p$ is odd, $p \bmod 4 \in \{1,3\}$. Both cases occur infinitely often.

This is the best possible elementary result for mod-4 residues: Dirichlet's theorem in full generality (for all moduli) requires analytic machinery, but the mod-4 case is completely accessible by elementary means.
